name: p-modeling
description: Design concurrent or retrying code with a P model checked by snappea, then test the real implementation against what the model found.
---

# P modeling

P finds bugs that only appear in some orderings: two clients read the same version,
a retry arrives after the state changed, a step fails between read and write. Use it
for shared state, retries, concurrency and recovery. Pure transformations need only
ordinary tests.

The model is worth what it changes in the code and tests. Follow these steps in order.

## 1. List the risks (before any code)

Write down, in `DESIGN.md`:

- the contract in checkable sentences ("a retried request returns its first result and
  has no further effect");
- the real atomic primitives (one compare-and-swap on one key, a lock, a transaction).
  Everything else can interleave;
- 5-10 concrete scenarios that could break the contract. Always consider:
  two clients that read the same version; a retry after another request changed the
  state (including retries of rejected or empty results); two objects sharing one
  store; each precondition false on its own; values exactly at each boundary.

## 2. Model the algorithm, not the API

- One machine for the store, holding exactly what the real store holds. Its handlers
  are the real primitives: `load` replies with (version, value); `cas` succeeds only at
  the current version.
- Client machines run your algorithm: send load, receive, decide, send cas, retry on
  failure. Every `send`/`receive` is a point where another client can run. If the
  whole operation is one handler, the model assumes the race away.
- A `spec` monitor computes the expected results from the contract and the history of
  requests, independently of the algorithm, and asserts each actual result.
- Drive it with 2-3 clients and small `choose(n)` inputs, plus fixed tests for the
  scenarios from step 1. Start from the [syntax reference](reference/p-patterns.md)
  and [CAS + retries example](examples/cas-retry/Balance.p).

## 3. Check until it passes for real

```sh
snappea check            # every test case, then coverage and mutation checks
```

- Exit 1 is work to do: a bug (fix the design; keep the scenario), a coverage gap
  (add a scenario), or a surviving mutant (an assertion is missing). Read each one.
- Do not finish with `--no-mutation` or `--allow-incomplete-coverage`. Use them only
  while iterating. If search is incomplete, shrink the bounds or raise `--timeout`.
- A bug found here is the payoff: write it down, fix the design, then implement.

## 4. Implement, then test what the model explored

Read [testing the implementation](guides/testing-implementation.md). For each
scenario and each bug the model found, write a Python test that makes it happen on the
real code. Random thread stress rarely hits a race; force it:

- wrap the store so a competing call runs between this call's load and its
  compare-and-swap, or so two calls read the same version before either writes;
- retry a request after another request changed the state, through a second object.

Add an observation test: run real calls, record their actual arguments and results as
events, and check them against your P spec with `snappea.check_events` (install
`pysnappea`, `import snappea`). See [implementation](guides/implementation.md).

## 5. Prove the tests can fail

Break your implementation on purpose, one change at a time (ignore the
compare-and-swap result, drop a retry memo, flip a boundary `<` to `<=`, keep state
in the object instead of the store). Run the tests each time; every break must fail a
test. Add a test for any that pass. Restore the code.

## Done means

- `snappea check` exits 0, with complete search or stated bounds.
- `python -m pytest` passes, including forced-interleaving and observation tests.
- Every hand-made break from step 5 fails a test.
- `DESIGN.md` states the contract, primitives, scenarios, model bounds, what the model
  found, and what is not covered.

## References

- [Syntax and commands](reference/p-patterns.md), [modeling](guides/modeling.md),
  [scenarios and oracles](guides/scenarios-and-oracles.md), [recovery](guides/recovery.md).
- Examples: [CAS + generated retries](examples/cas-retry/Balance.p),
  [reservation + Python tests](examples/reservation/Reservation.p),
  [generated histories](examples/bounded-history/bounded-history.p),
  [durable retry](examples/durable-retry/DurableRetry.p),
  [versioned publication](examples/versioned-publication/Revalidated.p).

# Lock service with fencing tokens

Implement `LockService` and `Resource` in `solution.py`, keeping all state in
`runtime.Store` (see `runtime.py`).

```python
LockService(store, ttl: int)
acquire(client: str, now: int) -> int | None
release(client: str, token: int, now: int) -> bool

Resource(store, name: str)
write(token: int, value: str) -> bool
read() -> str | None
```

- `acquire` grants the lock when no one holds an unexpired lease, and returns a fencing
  token. A lease granted at `now` expires at `now + ttl`; it is expired for any
  `now >= now + ttl`. Tokens are integers that strictly increase over the life of the
  store. If `client` already holds the unexpired lease, `acquire` returns that lease's
  token. Otherwise it returns `None`.
- `release` ends the lease if `client` holds the lease with `token` and it is unexpired at
  `now`, and returns whether it did.
- A `Resource` is protected by fencing: `write` rejects (returns `False`, no effect) a
  token that was never issued, or a token lower than one already used for an accepted
  write to that resource. Otherwise it stores `value` and returns `True`.
- Many `LockService` and `Resource` objects in many threads may share one `Store`; all
  `LockService` objects for a store use the same `ttl`. Callers supply `now`, and calls
  from different clients may arrive with out-of-order times.

Use P to model the design before implementing it, and to test the implementation.
`snappea` and the `pysnappea` Python package are installed. Keep your P files and
tests in this directory; the tests must run with `python -m pytest`.

# Test the implementation against what the model explored

The model checks every ordering of its clients. The implementation's tests should
make the same orderings happen on purpose. Starting threads and hoping rarely does:
a race window of a few microseconds is almost never hit.

Runnable example: [forced-interleaving](../examples/forced-interleaving/test_wallet.py).

## Force the interleaving

Wrap the real store in the test; the implementation does not change.

- **Both read the same version.** The first two `load` calls wait on a
  `threading.Barrier(2)`, then return. Both callers decide from the same state, and one
  compare-and-swap must fail and retry. Catches: ignoring the compare-and-swap result,
  deciding twice from one read, lost updates.
- **A competitor between read and write.** Right after this caller's first `load`,
  run a complete competing call against the inner store. This caller's
  compare-and-swap fails; on retry it must re-read and re-decide (now maybe reject).
  Catches: retrying with the stale value, re-checking only the version.

Assert both the returned results and the state afterwards, read through the public
API. With per-key stores, arm the wrapper only for the key under test.

## Replay requests after the state changed

For every operation that remembers a result, retry it after a different request
changed the state:

- retry an accepted request after its effect was undone by others (no second effect);
- retry a rejected or empty result after the reason went away (still rejected/empty);
- retry through a second object on the same store (the memo must live in the store);
- use the same request ID for two different operation kinds, if they are separate.

## Boundaries and preconditions

- Test each value exactly at, just below and just above each limit (capacity, expiry
  time, token order).
- For each acceptance condition, make only that condition false. When two conditions
  fail at once, one check can hide a missing other check.

## Check real calls against the P spec

Record actual arguments and results of real calls as events, then check them with the
same spec monitor the model uses:

```python
from snappea import check_events

events = []
ok = wallet.spend("a", 7)
events.append({"event": "eSpent", "payload": {"id": "a", "amount": 7, "ok": ok}})
events.append({"event": "eBalance", "payload": {"balance": wallet.balance()}})
check_events(events, "WalletContract", spec_files=["Wallet.p"], strict=True)
```

- Record in the test (as above) or `emit` from the application inside
  `snappea.check_spec(...)`; see [implementation](implementation.md).
- Record only what really happened: actual results and public reads, in the order the
  calls returned. Under real concurrency, return order is not commit order; use the
# Check actual implementation behavior

## Capture and check

- Install `pysnappea`; import `snappea`.
- Emit after meaningful committed changes, with relevant IDs, values, and versions.
- Partition by independent history; operations sharing an invariant must reach the same monitor instance.
- Save the observation test with implementation tests so later changes rerun it.

```python
from snappea import check_spec
from storage import ReservationStore


def test_competing_reservations():
    with check_spec(
        "Capacity",
        spec_files=["Reservation.p"],
        strict=True,
        check_hot=True,
        unknown_events="error",
    ):
        store = ReservationStore(1)  # emits eOpened
        first = store.read()
        second = store.read()
        assert store.reserve_if_unchanged("order-a", 1, first)
        assert not store.reserve_if_unchanged("order-b", 1, second)
```

- `check_spec` captures application `emit` calls; it does not intercept arbitrary methods. `check_events(events, "Capacity", spec_files=[...])` checks an existing recording.
- Without application emission, wrap real calls and record actual inputs, results, and public reads. Do not invent internal commits. Hand-written traces test only the monitor.
- Preserve distinctions: mapping all noninitial heads to one value can hide wrong results.
- See [reservation](../examples/reservation/Reservation.p) for saved tests, a rejected defective implementation, and an independent Python invariant.

## Evidence limits

- `strict=True` fails when a selected spec receives no relevant events; it cannot prove every operation emitted.
- `unknown_events="error"` rejects undeclared/misspelled names. CLI observation defaults to ignoring unknown events; declared events ignored by a spec are unchecked by it.
- `check_hot=True` checks unfinished monitor obligations at history end; observation does not explore application schedules.
- Emission before commit does not prove commit. Post-commit emission can be lost on crash.
- Concurrent post-commit emitters can reorder records. Order-sensitive checks need a version/sequence captured at the atomic operation or a controlled test boundary.
- Join child processes before checking their recordings; isolate each test/history. Event `src` identifies its emitting call site in failures.
- Runtime emitters must remain best-effort: no raised errors or blocked requests. Operational evidence should expose drops; explicit tests should validate recordings and fail on violations.

## Maintain correspondence

- Compare real reads, writes, atomicity, version checks, retries, and persistence with the model. Fix mismatches or justify equivalent primitives.
- Use observed monitor coverage to select missing application tests; model coverage measures different evidence.
- Keep direct boundary, concurrency, and crash tests. Test encoded record limits and valid logical operations exceeding one record, including after history grows.
- A passing observation validates the delivered history against the monitor, not missing events, unobserved schedules, or assumptions.
- Options: [Python helpers](https://github.com/crowecawcaw/snappea/blob/main/python/src/snappea/__init__.py), [strict observation](https://github.com/crowecawcaw/snappea/blob/main/docs/observe.md#strict-observation).

setsid nohup snappea check --timeout 100s --mutation-timeout 900s > /work/full2.txt 2>&1 < /dev/null &
cat > DESIGN.md <<'EOF'
# Lock service with fencing tokens: design

## Contract
1. `acquire` grants iff no unexpired lease at `now` (a lease granted at `g` is expired for `now >= g+ttl`); it returns a fresh token, strictly greater than every earlier token of the store.
2. If the caller already holds the unexpired lease, `acquire` returns that lease's token (no new token, no state change); otherwise `None`.
3. `release(client, token, now)` succeeds iff the lease is held by `client` with `token` and unexpired at `now`; any other call has no effect.
4. `Resource.write(token, v)` is rejected, with no effect, if the token was never issued (`token < 1` or `> last issued`) or is lower than a token already used for an accepted write to that resource; equal tokens are accepted.
5. Rejected writes do not raise the resource's mark. Resources of different names are independent.
6. Tokens never go down, even after release or expiry.

## Atomic primitives
Only `Store.load(key)` and `Store.compare_swap(key, version, value)` on one key. No cross-key transaction. So:
- `"lock"` holds `{last, holder, token, exp}` in one record: lease and token counter change in one CAS, so a fresh token cannot be handed out twice. `last` is never reset by release/expiry.
- `"resource:<name>"` holds `{high, value}` in one record: the fence check and the value update are one CAS.
- `Resource.write` reads `"lock"` and the resource record separately. This is safe because `last` only grows: a token seen as issued stays issued. A token seen as unissued is rejected, which linearizes at that read.
- All state is in the store; no per-object state (second objects on one store behave the same).

## Scenarios (risks)
1. Two clients acquire having read the same version: exactly one wins.
2. Competitor re-acquires between my load (saw expired) and my CAS: I must redecide and get `None`.
3. Expiry boundary: `now == exp-1` live, `now == exp` expired; holder re-acquiring at `exp` gets a new token.
4. Release races: wrong client only, wrong token only, expired only, already released, lease changed between load and CAS.
5. Release followed by acquire: token must still increase (counter kept in the record).
6. Write with token never issued (0, negative, above last, nothing issued) must not raise the mark.
7. Write with lower token after higher accepted; equal token; competing higher write between my load and CAS.
8. Two writes read the same resource version.
9. Two resources and two service objects on one store.
10. Out-of-order `now` between clients.

## Model (`Lock.p`)
Store machine = lock record + resource record with load/CAS handlers; `Client.run` runs the real algorithm with send/receive at every step. `FenceContract` (spec) computes expected results from the contract and commit history, independently of the algorithm: read-only outcomes are checked against the oracle state at the load, writes at commit; every client reply must equal that. Tests: `tcGenLease` (acquire at 3 times, then generated acquire/release vs a generated op of client 2; ttl 2, tokens 1..2), `tcGenFence` (two clients acquire at generated times, then write generated tokens 0..3), `tcExpiry`, `tcRelease` (fixed boundary scenarios). Bounds: 2 clients, <=3 ops total per generated test (3 ops each in fixed ones), times 0..4, tokens 0..3, ttl 2, one resource. Searches completed for all four.

## What the model found
No design bug in the final design. While modelling, the key decision was forced by the primitives: the token counter must live in the same record as the lease (a separate counter key would allow duplicate or non-monotone tokens), and write must read `last` before the resource record so "issued" is monotone.

## Implementation tests (`test_solution.py`, `Observed.p`)
Forced interleavings via store wrappers (same-version barrier, competitor between load and CAS), boundary tests, retries through second objects, and an observation test that records real call arguments/results and checks them with `check_events` against `ObservedContract` (sequential contract spec, ttl 2). 24 hand-made breaks (ignored CAS, `<`/`<=` flips, dropped checks, counter reset, shared key, state kept in the object) each fail a test.

## Not covered
Read is trivial and unmodelled. Real thread timing beyond forced interleavings; more than 2 clients, ttl other than 2 in the model; store failures/crash; `now` values far apart in the model (0..4 only); the observation spec checks sequential histories, not concurrent commit order.
EOF
